# History of Transfer Fallback and Account Credentials

## Initial Record (2023-08)

This page was first created because `boto3/s3/transfer.py` had come up in two lines of investigation: one looking at automatic transfer manager fallback, the other at how the account ID continued to propagate with credentials. Both could be approached from the transfer configuration area, but at the time there was no evidence that they converged in the same branch.

The working assessment at the time was: when the configuration does not explicitly specify a client, try the faster transfer path first; if that path is unavailable, fall back to the classic manager. "Unavailable" had not yet been broken down into implementation capabilities, runtime environment, and instance optimization status, so this was not enough to determine which condition callers should check.

The account ID investigation was even less complete. The note said only "needs to be passed along with credentials," with no object names, caller examples, or results. Someone suggested changing account ID propagation and the transfer manager together, on the grounds that a single change would make integration testing easier; but this was only a way to bundle the changes, not a confirmed call relationship.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

1. Fix the transfer implementation in `TransferConfig`. Simple to implement, but adding a new client would require changes to callers.
2. Keep the choice open and put the decision about which manager is actually used in `create_transfer_manager`. Fewer caller changes, but logs and tests would need to show which path was ultimately used.
3. Submit account ID propagation and fallback together. This consolidates the scope, but at the time there were no account objects, credential objects, or call results to check against.

Keep the second approach for now. Account ID propagation is not included in this decision and remains a separate item to verify. The source-code entry point was recorded only as `boto3/s3/transfer.py`; "can be reached from here" was not written as "is handled here."

## Open Questions

- The public wording for the fallback conditions has not been finalized.
- There are no test examples for the account ID propagation path.
- A hands-on check is needed to confirm the relationship between the default configuration and the classic manager.
- It has not yet been decided whether logs should record the configured choice or the actual object after creation.

# Transport Fallback and Account Credential History

## Legacy Entry Point

This page originally had only one file entry point and two working assessments. The issue name pointed to `boto3/s3/transfer.py`, so the early notes listed the transport configuration, manager creation, and Account Identifier Credential Propagation side by side. Looking back later showed that being listed side by side did not make them the same thing: the former at least had a configuration object to compare against, while the latter at the time had only a user path still to be filled in.

The decision recorded in the year 2023 remains valid: do not pin a specific transport implementation in every caller. Have `TransferConfig` store the choice first, then have `create_transfer_manager` handle the actual implementation. This decision settled ownership of the entry point, but it did not define the failure criteria precisely enough. It also did not prove that the account identifier passes through the same object chain.

There were three ways to structure this at the time. The first was to hard-code the classic implementation. This was easiest for integrators to understand, but made the choice in the configuration meaningless; adding implementations later would also require repeated changes at call sites. The second was to centralize the capability check at manager creation. This preserved the configuration layer's room for choice, so callers did not need to duplicate implementation checks. The third was to put account-identifier propagation and fallback into a single change. That would make scheduling easier, but would tie together one workstream with a configuration entry and another with no result sample.

Keep option two. Here, "keep" only means that the responsibility location has been decided; it does not mean that all external wording for the fallback conditions has been finalized.

## 2024-01 Review Addendum

The review revisited three things: whether the configuration stores the user's choice, whether implementation capability is still checked when the manager is created, and whether the object obtained after fallback is still a transport manager. The review did not produce a complete call graph, but confirmed that "no CRT" cannot be directly written as "the entire transport function failed." At minimum, an unavailable optional implementation must be distinguished from the classic path itself being unavailable.

This changed the wording of option two. The original "try the faster path first" sounded too much like an inevitable runtime action, making it easy for integrators to understand fallback as exception recovery. Safer wording is: the configuration retains room for choice, and the manager creation point determines the actual implementation. As for the precise relationship among the default value, capability check, and returned object, the review record did not have enough output at the time to sign off on each item individually.

> First decide who owns the choice, then decide what the logs should say. Don't casually fold the account identifier into the fallback conclusion.

This short phrase from the review discussion was retained. It explains why the two lines were not merged in this version, and why the logging issue cannot in turn prove where credential propagation occurs.

## Original Paragraph Retained

> When no client is explicitly specified, the caller should use the classic transport manager directly; if CRT is enabled in the future, the caller can change the parameter.

**Deprecated (wording from the 2023 initial draft).** This passage was not deleted because it records why someone initially suggested adding a check at the caller. After review, it is no longer used to plan integration: putting the check at the caller would expose implementation capability to every call site and still would not show whether the account identifier continues to propagate along the same object chain.

One more short note is retained:

> The account identifier probably propagates after manager creation; start looking in that direction.

**Later overturned as a working hypothesis.** This sentence gives only a search order; it provides no caller-side evidence. It cannot serve as a decision about where propagation occurs. The account identifier still needs to be checked separately against a result; do not use the transport fallback decision to fill in that gap.

## Decision and Gaps in This Version

This version still uses the option that preserves room for choice. External-facing materials need to spell out the default choice, the behavior when an implementation is unavailable, and the returned object separately. This review has not yet turned these three into final public-facing sentences, so vague wording is not presented here as a specification.

The account identifier remains separate. The only thing that can be confirmed is that it is adjacent to the entry point; it cannot be confirmed whether propagation occurs during configuration copying, manager creation, or a further-downstream request-preparation stage. The next review needs to bring back a caller-side result, rather than continuing to infer from filenames.

## Old Note: Put the Two Threads Together First

In month 8 of 2023, this page did not begin with a complete design. All that was at hand was a file entry point and two names that were easily glossed over in the same sentence: transport manager fallback, Account Identifier Credential Propagation. So the earliest notes listed them side by side under `boto3/s3/transfer.py`.

The original note was written in a hurry: when the configuration does not specify an implementation, try the available fast path first; if that fails, use the classic manager. For the account identifier, it said only "must be passed along with the credentials," with no object name, no caller example, and no results to check against. The decision at the time was narrow in scope: simply to prevent each caller from choosing its own transport implementation. Whether the account identifier went through the same creation path was left blank.

This initial wording remains in the archive, not because it was accurate, but because it records where the first disagreement began. It placed "implementation selection" and "identity propagation" too close together, so several later reviews first spent time separating the two. The early file index only put the issue name in the path, without further explaining the relationships among fields, objects, and callers; therefore, no conclusion about propagation can be inferred from the filename itself.

Four candidate approaches were visible at the time. First, fix a single implementation in `TransferConfig`, so callers would no longer face that choice. Second, retain the choice in the configuration and create the final manager at a centralized entry point. Third, have each caller check transport capabilities first, then decide whether to use the classic implementation. Fourth, submit account identifier propagation and fallback together, addressing both threads in a single compatibility change.

The initial notes favored the second approach, but recorded it only as a working decision, without claiming it had been validated. Fixing the implementation would make the entry point straightforward, at the cost of having to modify callers one by one when switching clients later. Decentralized checks would keep logs close to the point of use, at the cost of duplicating the interpretation of capability conditions across entry points. Bundling in the account identifier appeared to save one round of scheduling, but at the time there was not even an example showing at what stage propagation occurred, so it could not be treated as the same behavior as manager fallback.

At the time, only `boto3/s3/transfer.py` was listed as the source-code entry point. The repository index classified this path as an existing Python module, for reading the code and checking historical behavior. It could help locate the file again, but could not substitute for the object relationships in the decision record. This limitation reflected the actual state of the early material, not a statement of evidence added later.

## Additional Notes from the Review Table

From the end of 2023 to month 1 of 2024, the review focused on locations adjacent to `TransferConfig` and `create_transfer_manager`. The review first asked "who is responsible for choosing", not "which client is faster". If callers directly pin the classic implementation, the selection in the configuration becomes ineffective; if callers are responsible for assessing implementation capabilities, new entry points will also have to duplicate the same conditions. Centralizing the decision where the manager is created at least keeps callers from having to know these implementation details.

The centralized approach was ultimately retained, but it was not presented as a full API commitment. The review addendum confirmed only two points: callers are not responsible for duplicating the implementation selection logic; "no CRT" cannot simply be written as "transport failure". There was no test output available to cite at the time, so the relationship between the default value and the returned object was not included in v2, nor was a particular status in the logs used as a substitute for the actual returned object.

A short remark from the meeting was also preserved:

> First decide who is responsible for choosing, then decide what the logs should say. Do not casually fold account identifiers into the fallback conclusion.

This remark later influenced how the page was divided into sections. Here, the options and decisions for transport fallback are retained, while the question of account identifiers is only settled when actual call results are available. It is not a conclusion about the internal structure of credentials, just the review's requirement at the time for the order of evidence.

Another review comment was that configuration values, capability assessments, and creation results must not be collapsed into the single phrase "fast path failure". This comment did not produce a complete call graph, but it changed how things were recorded: subsequent addenda documented configuration selection, implementation availability, and the returned object separately, to avoid inferring the other two from any one of them.

## The incorrect proposal that was retained

> When no client is explicitly specified, the caller should directly use the classic transport manager; if CRT needs to be enabled in the future, the caller should then change the parameters.

**Deprecated, with the original paragraph retained.** This was a recommendation in the initial draft of 2023, not the current integration instructions. Its problem was not just that it favored the classic implementation, but that it also made "enabling it in the future" the caller's responsibility. If it continued to be followed, call sites would have to know the underlying capabilities; the same `TransferConfig` might also be interpreted differently at different entry points. It once seemed suitable for short-term compatibility, but it cannot support unified selection as more transport implementations are added.

The old paragraph was not rewritten into a correct version, because that would erase an actual change made during review. When reading it now, treat it as the candidate proposal and the reasons against it at the time, rather than inferring current behavior from the word "should" in the sentence. It also explains why the search in the early materials went back and forth among the three locations of caller, configuration, and manager.

There was also a shorter old note that was not deleted:

> Account identifier propagation probably occurs after the manager is created, so start by looking in that direction.

**Later rejected as a working hypothesis.** This statement has no corresponding caller-side evidence. It can indicate the search order at the time, but it cannot determine where propagation occurred. The account-identifier thread remains an adjacent issue on this page; do not use the transport-fallback conclusion to fill it in.

This old hypothesis led to a very specific misreading: seeing that both topics begin in the same file makes it easy to mistake manager creation for the boundary of credential propagation. Later records clearly distinguish between "entry-point adjacency" and "propagation has already occurred." The former can be retained; the latter requires a caller-side result. This distinction is also retained in the old appendix, making it easier to explain why an incorrect search direction emerged early.

## What One Review Did Not Resolve

The review in 2024 examined "default configuration," "implementation availability," and "returned manager type" separately, but did not produce a complete call graph. The findings were sufficient to reject the proposal that the caller hard-code the classic implementation, but still insufficient to explain the logs in all environments. In particular, do not conflate the absence of CRT in a given environment with the instance optimization state; if these states need to be described externally, cite the runtime output from that time directly instead of turning state names into an inference.

The review also did not confirm whether transport implementation selection uses the same configuration object at every entry point. This issue was not expanded into a new design item at the time because the existing materials only provided the file entry point and adjacent declarations. It was noted separately because caller behavior would affect subsequent examples; but before results were available, it could not be used to change the already-decided responsibility boundary.

The review of the account identifier stopped earlier. The known entry point is still the same transport module; the unconfirmed points include: whether the credentials already carry the account identifier, whether propagation occurs before or after parameter copying, and whether the caller's result can display it. No additional speculation is added here, and the card's to-do items are not written as completed actions.

At the time, someone suggested first using whether transport fallback occurred to determine whether the account identifier had been transmitted successfully. This suggestion was not retained as an operational step. Fallback is a result of implementation selection, while the account identifier is the object being propagated with the credentials; the two may appear in the same user path, but one result cannot serve as evidence for the other. The review therefore downgraded this suggestion to a convenience check that was not adopted.

## Field Recheck in 2025

By year 2025, month 9, the record for SDK-201 showed `qa_reproduced`, then changed to `work_started` on month 9, day 8. This turned "automatic transport manager fallback" from an early search term into a work item requiring rechecking against the original configuration; it did not prove the account identifier's propagation location for this page. The two state changes also did not provide a caller-side result that could be directly transferred here, so they are preserved only in the recheck timeline.

The account identifier workstream was still in the investigation stage as late as month 10. SDK-215 had a `qa_reproduced` record on day 10 of month 10, and moved into `work_started` on day 13 of month 10. The card itself also requires using existing tests or examples to exercise user paths that are not yet covered and writing the results back to the card. Here "reproduction" only shows that someone performed a check along the path, it cannot be expanded into a claim that propagation is complete, nor can the work item status be treated as an implementation decision.

These two follow-up check dates do not mean that the same thing was verified twice. SDK-201 concerns the automatic transfer manager fallback; SDK-215 concerns Account Identifier Credential Propagation. They appear side by side in this record because they historically started at the same file entry point, not because the cards have already established a shared underlying branch.

The on-site follow-up check also preserved a practical writing constraint: for transfer defaults, the original names of the configuration fields and creation entry points must be used; for account identifiers, the observed entry points must be documented separately from what remains unconfirmed downstream. This lets readers refer back separately to SDK-201, SDK-215, without treating the two cards as a single release decision.

## Archiving the Options One by One

### Hard-code the classic manager

The advantage is straightforward behavior, with almost no need for existing callers to understand capability detection. The drawbacks had already surfaced in the early review: the implementation choice in the configuration would become ineffective, and future client switches would require changes to callers; it would also leave no explanation for retaining the transfer implementation selection layer. Not adopted.

This option could also reduce branching in logging in the short term, because every entry point would see only the classic implementation. But this would merely move the differences from manager creation to callers, without establishing whether different callers use the same configuration. The review did not find sufficient reason to take on this distributed maintenance cost, so the old text remains as historical material and is no longer used as a basis for integration.

### Make callers responsible for evaluating CRT

The advantage is that logging can stay close to the call site, while the drawback is that the checks would be spread across multiple entry points. This option would also turn runtime environment details into public integration requirements. The 2023 note once favored it, but it was marked as abandoned after the 2024 review.

It was not adopted, but not because logs have no value. Logs may still help reveal the selection outcome, but observation through logs and responsibility for selection are different issues. The current record places "who determines the actual manager" at the creation entry point, and leaves "which runtime states to record" to materials that contain output; when there is no output, no state is filled in.

### Commit account identifier propagation and fallback together

The advantage is that the changes appear focused. The disadvantage is that the two tracks have different evidence: fallback has configuration and a manager entry point, while the account identifier has only a user path that still needs to be filled in. There is not enough material to tie them into a single decision, so wording that combined them into one conclusion was not adopted.

Putting the two topics in one commit also poses a risk for the historical record: later readers may mistake the object returned by the transport implementation for the result of credential propagation. The early notes had already brought these topics close together, which is precisely why this version keeps the explanations separate. This does not judge whether the two changes can be carried out concurrently from an engineering perspective; it only records that they were not signed off as a single decision at the time.

### Preserve flexibility in selection, with the creation entry point determining the actual implementation

This remains the current direction. It does not require callers to duplicate the selection logic, and it also allows the behavior when an implementation is unavailable to be documented near the creation entry point. It does not automatically answer the account identifier propagation question; that still requires a separate caller-side result.

Over time, the wording of this option became narrower. The early wording was "try the fast path first," which later became "the configuration preserves flexibility in selection, and the creation entry point handles the actual implementation," and only at the end were the default value and the object returned in the unavailable case stated precisely. The initial wording must not replace the final description of the behavior, nor can the account identifier track also be treated as complete merely because the final sentence has been settled.

## 2025-12 Current conclusion

As of month 12 of 2025, the precise behavior of transport selection is stated in the following sentence, placed after four or more layers of historical records; it must not be replaced with the early "try the fast path first" wording:

When no transport implementation has been explicitly selected, the default value of TransferConfig.preferred_transfer_client must be auto; if CRT is unavailable, create_transfer_manager still returns the classic transport manager.

This sentence is this page's current definitive statement on transport fallback. It ties the default value to `TransferConfig.preferred_transfer_client` and the behavior when unavailable to `create_transfer_manager`, and also makes clear that the fallback result is not a branch that returns a failure to the caller. It does not claim that CRT necessarily exists, nor does it incorporate the instance's optimization state into the definition of the default value.

The decision here covers only the behavior between two explicitly identified elements: the default configuration field and the result of creating a manager. It does not include `Credentials`, account identifiers, or further downstream request preparation in the same proposition. This is deliberate, because the account identifier track has not obtained caller-side results at the same level of precision. Reaching a precise conclusion does not mean expanding the scope.

In external-facing materials, if the question is "what configuration is used when none is explicitly selected", check `TransferConfig.preferred_transfer_client`; if the question is "what was created when CRT was unavailable", check `create_transfer_manager`. If the question shifts to account identifiers, these two object names cannot directly answer where propagation occurs. File paths remain starting points for checking back, but are not evidence of credential propagation.

## Boundary Between the Current Decision and Adjacent Issues

The decision on transport fallback has moved from an early working assessment to an explicit position: callers do not pin the classic implementation, and the transport entry point explains the default configuration and creation result. Account Identifier Credential Propagation has not been declared complete on this page. The to-do for SDK-215 still applies: existing tests or examples need to be used to exercise user paths not yet covered, and the results need to be written back to the card.

If subsequent results show that propagation occurs before the transport configuration is copied, a new caller-facing record should be added; if the results only show values after the manager is created, only that observation can be recorded, and the earlier configuration stage cannot be inferred from it. Neither outcome should rewrite the transport statements already finalized on this page. Both possible directions are retained here because the current materials do not select either one.

Account identifiers may also be related to the credential object itself, rather than just the manager object. The existing records do not list that object's fields or methods to call, so this page does not fill in a seemingly complete chain. What can be confirmed is that the question began at the transport module entry point, and the card still calls for exercising user paths; what cannot be confirmed is the specific point of propagation, the form of the result, and whether it occurs at the same time as fallback.

This distinction also constrains how subsequent materials are archived. New transport observations can update the follow-up checks associated with SDK-201, but cannot automatically close SDK-215; new account identifier results can be added to the credential propagation record, but cannot in turn change the default transport selection. The two cards are related in navigation, but remain separate in their decisions.

## Excerpts from Previous Sessions

The following excerpts are brief remarks left during previous maintenance rounds, not new specifications:

- "First check what `TransferConfig` stores, then check what the creation entry point receives."
- "Not having CRT does not mean the transport functionality as a whole has no exit."
- "Hold off on signing off on account identifiers together with fallback."
- "A filename can lead you to the scene, but it cannot make decisions on the scene's behalf."

The first sentence preserves the early lookup order, the second sentence is a correction to the old attribution from 2024 year, the third sentence explains why the two cards still moved forward separately in 2025 year, and the fourth sentence is a later supplement on the limitations of path indexing. Their purpose is to preserve how the judgment changed, not to replace the current position. The excerpts were not consolidated into a unified glossary because they are maintenance traces from different periods.

The second sentence is easy to misread as "any environment without CRT can run directly." That is not what it means; at the time, it was only arguing against describing an unavailable optional implementation as a failure of the entire transport function. The current precise wording has already limited the scope to the default choice and the creation result, so readers should not use the excerpt to extrapolate unrecorded environment behavior.

## Appendix: Old Examples

### Old Example A: The Caller Directly Specifies the Classic Implementation

This is the easiest old example to copy. It does not explain why the configuration still needs to retain the implementation choice, nor does it cover changes in the availability of CRT. **Obsolete; do not add new call sites based on this example.** The example remains in the appendix because this kind of recommendation really did appear first in early search results.

This example was once treated as a way to reduce compatibility risk: if all callers choose the classic manager, then on the surface there is no need to understand the other client. But it shifts responsibility for choosing the configuration to the caller and makes each subsequent call site decide for itself what "available" means. That is precisely why the review later stopped accepting it. The appendix preserves why it was attractive at the time, not to add current support for it.

### Old Example B: Treating the Account Identifier as a Fallback Signal

An old note once used the wording "if fallback occurs, check the account identifier while you're at it." **Unverified; cannot be used as a step.** Fallback is the result of selecting a transport implementation, while the account identifier is a verification target for credential propagation; for now, neither can prove the other.

It still has archival value because it explains why the two lines were initially written together. Without a result from the caller, a single return from the classic manager cannot be used to infer that the account identifier has propagated, nor can seeing the account identifier be used to infer that fallback occurred. This example should not be rewritten as a troubleshooting sequence.

### Old Example C: Recording Only the Filename, Not the Entry Point

Early materials retained only `boto3/s3/transfer.py`, and `TransferConfig` and `create_transfer_manager` were added later. The filename remains a navigation entry point, but the determining dependencies are the fields and the creation action. This old example explains why this page no longer uses paths alone in place of behavior descriptions.

It also illustrates the scope of this page. The path comes from the `v_prev` record of `internal/SDK`, which can support returning to the file location at that time; it cannot, by itself, support determining at which layer account identifier propagation occurred. The old example is no longer a recommended format, but it is retained here to explain why later versions gradually added object names.

### Old Example D: Writing the Conclusion First, Then Looking for the Corresponding Object

During later maintenance, another tendency emerged: first writing "fallback after fast-path failure" into the summary, then going back to look for configuration fields. This sequence was not retained as a formal step. It puts runtime impressions ahead of object relationships, and can easily turn instance-level optimizations, implementation capabilities, and returned results into an undifferentiated causal chain.

The current version therefore places the precise formulation after the historical layer, and retains the earlier formulation as superseded material. This lets readers see how the conclusion gradually narrowed through option comparisons, review gaps, and on-site rechecks, rather than disguising the notes from 2023 as final rules that were already known at the time.

## Trace-back diagram

The diagram below shows only the local adjacencies confirmed in the records, without filling in an unknown chain of account identifier propagation:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> config
    config: TransferConfig
    config --> manager
    manager: create_transfer_manager
    manager --> classic: CRT unavailable
    classic: Classic transport manager
    classic --> [*]
```

The `config` and `manager` in the diagram are two entry-point names that have stabilized in the records; "CRT unavailable" marks only the branch explicitly covered by the current decision; the account identifier is not shown, because the existing material does not confirm whether it belongs before configuration copying, after manager creation, or in the request preparation phase. The diagram cannot replace the user-path results that still need to be added for SDK-215.

## Trace-back locations

Trace transport fallback from [SDK-201], and Account Identifier Credential Propagation from [SDK-215]; the source-code entry point is `boto3/s3/transfer.py`. Each card provides its own on-site navigation and historical work status, while the current transport decision remains in this history document.

# S3 Transfer Compatibility Trial Plan

Start by trying two adjacent changes around `boto3/s3/transfer.py` that should not be tightly coupled: a version gate for the optional CRT path, and how text is constructed when debug logging is disabled. At this stage, leave users' existing transfer configuration unchanged, and don't turn normal transfer selection into a version-policy experiment.

The working assumption for the version gate is that it only affects the optimized branch that depends on CRT. If the conditions aren't met, fall back to the existing classic path rather than causing the entire transfer entry point to fail. The risk identified so far is that version strings may not always be suitable for lexicographic comparison; padding, leading zeros, or values with additional tags could all cause a simple comparison to produce incorrect results.

There are two candidate approaches for logging. One is to build the complete status string before making the debug logging call; the other is to pass the format string and arguments directly to the logging call, allowing text formatting to be skipped when debug logging is disabled. The preference is the latter, but first confirm that these call sites don't use the preformatted string for anything other than logging.

The trial is limited to the version-gating branch and the immediately adjacent debug logging calls. The version check and logging approach must be independently reversible: if the former causes problems, restore the original candidate path; if the latter causes problems, restore the original call form.

Still needed: the actual forms of version inputs; which branch unrecognized versions should take; whether any call sites use diagnostic text as non-log data.

# S3 Transfer Compatibility Trial Plan

`boto3/s3/transfer.py` was initially treated as a small-scope compatibility cleanup: gate the optional CRT optimization while avoiding eager construction of diagnostic strings when debug logging is disabled. After reviewing the draft, we first need to drop an overly optimistic assumption: when version text looks well-formed, lexicographic comparison may happen to produce a sensible order, but that does not show that padded versions, additional tags, or inputs that cannot be converted will take the right branch.

String ordering is therefore no longer a candidate implementation. We are keeping the approach of first obtaining comparable semantic versions, then deciding whether the relevant optimization can be enabled. If an input cannot be converted, we should not keep guessing whether it is newer; it should take the branch that does not meet the threshold. This is a conservative choice: some environments will continue to use the existing path, but a parse failure will not let an optimization through without justification.

This gate does not redefine all the rules for selecting a transfer client. Dependency discovery, configuration already supplied by the user, and availability of the classic transfer path remain separate concerns. The version check only answers whether the discovered CRT meets the requirement. If a missing dependency, an outdated version, and an invalid version format are collapsed into a single state, troubleshooting will no longer distinguish installation issues from comparison issues, and log messages can become ambiguous as well.

The original draft's statement, "If it isn't recognized, we can still try as usual," is retained as a rejected approach. That would make the gate meaningless: the same unknown input cannot establish that the condition is met, yet could still enter an optimization branch that depends on that condition. If new version formats need to be supported later, explicit parsing rules should be added rather than exceptions that let unknown values pass. This proposal has not yet settled on a comparison utility or import method.

The logging trial is also scoped to call sites. The goal is not to reduce diagnostic content, much less overhaul the logging framework; it is to avoid string interpolation or concatenation for this one transfer diagnostic when debug logging is disabled. The format string and arguments should stay at the logging call site, with the same fields output in the same order when enabled. If a string has to be built first for a non-logging check or to pass elsewhere, do not mechanically replace that code; separate out that use first.

During the trial, distinguish at least three version outcomes: comparable and meets the threshold, comparable but does not meet the threshold, and uninterpretable. The third must not be hidden by defaulting to success. For logging, check call behavior with debug enabled and disabled. This only addresses when formatting happens and should not change return values, exception propagation, or client selection.

Rollback is split into two independent tracks. If semantic comparison causes an incorrect fallback in a supported environment, roll back the gate integration and restore the previous candidate selection; the logging changes do not need to be rolled back with it. If the way arguments are passed to logging affects existing diagnostics, restore the original code at that call site without changing the version branch. The remaining open questions are which S3 optimization entry points actually depend on the same CRT capability, and whether any legacy callers consume the diagnostic text.

# S3 Transfer Compatibility Trial Plan

This plan remains on the `boto3/s3/transfer.py` track. It covers two changes near transfer initialization: one determines whether to consider the optional CRT optimization; the other avoids building diagnostic text in advance when debug logging is disabled. Their proximity was why they were initially bundled together; they should now be treated as separate risks. The former changes compatibility checks, while the latter only changes when logging calls perform formatting. Releasing or rolling back either change must not depend on releasing or rolling back the other.

The earliest notes treated version values as plain text and assumed that values that "looked larger" could continue to try the optimization. That judgment has been discarded, but remains in historical revisions: it explains why version parsing later became necessary. Lexicographic ordering covers only some well-formed inputs; it does not establish how to handle padded versions, additional tags, or values that cannot be interpreted. Without a comparable result, continuing to try the optimization is not a neutral choice: it asserts, without evidence, that the threshold has been met.

The decision for this round is to use an explicit capability gate: CRT versions must be compared as semantic versions, and unparseable versions must be treated as failing the requirement; the minimum version for the relevant S3 optimization capability is 0.19.18. This rule governs only whether optimizations that depend on CRT are eligible. It must not be expanded into a master switch for all transfer requests. If the version meets the requirement, continue into the existing CRT candidate path; if it is too old or cannot be parsed, stay on the existing non-optimized path.

This distinction needs to remain in both the implementation and diagnostics. Whether CRT is present answers whether the dependency can be discovered; whether its version meets the requirement answers whether the discovered dependency can support a specific optimization. These checks often appear in the same initialization code, but should not be collapsed into a generic "unavailable." A missing dependency, an outdated version, and an abnormal version format call for different troubleshooting approaches. The version gate also does not replace users' existing transfer configuration choices; this adjustment does not rewrite the rules for user settings or classic-path selection.

Another, more permissive approach was considered: still treat CRT as a candidate to try when parsing fails, to reduce fallbacks. That approach was not adopted. It would turn a parsing failure into permission to use the optimization. If transfers then behaved unexpectedly, the selection result would not tell us whether the issue was installation, version, or format. The cost of the conservative branch is that some environments will not get the optimization; in return, unknown inputs will not be treated as having met the threshold. If new version tags need support in the future, add parsing rules and corresponding samples before changing this branch, rather than making exceptions for unknown values.

The trial scope for the version change must not be extrapolated from this one entry point, either. `boto3/s3/transfer.py` is the starting point for this investigation, not a declaration of responsibility for all S3 transfer behavior. If other optimization entry points are later found to use the same capability, confirm individually that they actually depend on the same CRT condition; do not share the gate just because the names are similar. This proposal only requires an explainable outcome for the candidate path here in each of three version cases: meets the requirement, does not meet it, and cannot be parsed.

The logging work retains the narrower goal from the second revision. The pattern to avoid is this: even with debug logging disabled, the call path first performs string interpolation, concatenation, or state-text construction, then hands the logging system a result that will never be emitted. Retaining the format string and arguments lets the logging call handle formatting when diagnostics actually need to be emitted, so that cost is incurred only with debug logging enabled.

This is not a plan to remove diagnostics. Client selection, version status, and instance-related state can still appear in the existing diagnostics; this change does not alter their field meanings or reorganize state from multiple places into a new summary message. During review, we discussed first assembling a single block of transfer state and then dispatching it at different log levels. That approach was not included because it would reintroduce formatting costs on the logging-disabled path and mix version checks, client selection, and instance state into a block of text that is hard to examine in parts.

Call sites also need an exception check: if text generated in advance at a call site is also consumed outside logging, that site cannot be switched directly to lazy formatting. It should stay as written until the text's other use has been explained separately. Conversely, only calls used for debug output are suitable for deferred formatting. This avoids turning a performance adjustment into a data-flow change, and avoids changing return values, exception propagation, or transfer client selection through the logging change.

Implementation remains a two-step process. First integrate semantic-version parsing and the conservative branch, and confirm that all three outcomes take their expected paths: meets the threshold, below the threshold, and cannot be parsed. Then update the adjacent debug calls and observe diagnostic behavior with debug logging enabled and disabled. Success with the version change does not prove the logging change is correct; unchanged logs do not prove version selection is correct either. The two changes share only a location, not validation conclusions.

Rollbacks are separate as well. If semantic comparison causes supported environments to fall back incorrectly, roll back the version-gate integration and restore the previous candidate selection; lazy log formatting can remain. If the logging call's argument form affects existing diagnostic text, restore the original call form at that site without changing the confirmed version paths. If either side requires expanding into a client-selection refactor or logging framework cleanup, stop at the scope boundary and propose a separate change.

Only two areas remain undecided: whether parseable versions with extra tags need their own rules, and which other S3 optimization entry points share the same capability gate as this one. The former needs verifiable version samples first; the latter needs confirmation of the actual dependencies. Neither should be assumed to have been covered in this round.

# Troubleshooting Client Context Parameters

When a service reference page shows the symptom "the regular request parameters are all there, but the group of parameters needed when initializing the client cannot be found", first pin down the symptom on the generated page. Do not infer the template from the link name the user sees, and do not attribute all documentation behavior to this file just because you see `boto3/docs/client.py`. This record preserves a troubleshooting tree for an old entry point, including a few earlier assessments that were never removed; the current verification entry point is in the latter half.

## 2023-11-14: The Initial Entry Point

The earliest surviving record contained only two things: both the issue name and the call name pointed to `boto3/docs/client.py`, and the file header showed:

```python
from botocore.docs.client import ClientDocumenter
```

The approach at the time was straightforward. Open the service reference page and search for the parameter name; if it cannot be found, follow `boto3/docs/client.py` back to the documentation generation entry point. No copy of the generated page was saved, and the headings and parameter groups in the template were not copied down. Because regular request members were still visible on the page, the initial working hypothesis was: the client context parameters had already been collected, but were listed after the regular request members, and the search order was not obvious.

This was only an on-the-spot assessment at the time, not the page contract confirmed later. If the same symptom is reproduced, first record the page address, service name, and parameter groups you see. If any of these is missing, stop at "entry point found"; do not fill in the page layout based on the path name.

## 2023 Year-End Operational Margin Note

A shortcut branch was once used while on call:

```text
Parameter name cannot be found
  ├─ Regular request members can be found: keep looking farther down in the same group
  └─ Regular request members cannot be found either: check the generated file
```

This tree addressed "where to start looking", not "which group the client context parameters should belong to". At the time, page navigation and body content were often viewed separately, and not finding a heading was treated as missing content. This margin note is retained because old links still bring people to this record; when you reach "keep looking farther down in the same group", stop and first confirm which objects the parameters apply to.

If the page only has regular request members, recording the following minimum information is enough:

- Whether the service reference page can be opened;
- The heading for the regular request members;
- Whether searching for the parameter name matches any other text;
- Whether the generated file for the page can be found locally.

Do not treat "the release notes do not mention it separately" as a page generation failure. Release notes, templates, and the final reference page are different surfaces to inspect.

## 2024-09-19: A Counterexample from the First Verification Pass

During verification, "cannot be found on the page" was split into two questions: whether the parameters were not generated, and whether they were generated but not placed in the expected section. The previous record had combined the two, leading to a temporary workaround of "merge them into the regular request parameter list first, so users can at least find them in a search".

This workaround has been abandoned. It changed the reader's understanding of parameter scope: regular request members describe what is submitted in a single call, while client context parameters describe the context passed in when creating the client. Similar names do not prove that they belong to the same group. Even if they can temporarily be found in a search on the page, their placement would still mislead callers.

The verification order was changed to: first inspect the headings on the generated page, then the field groups under those headings, and only then return to the source file to confirm navigation and dependencies. If the heading is absent but regular fields are present, provisionally record it as a page structure issue; if the heading is present but fields are missing, inspect the template inputs; only if the source file entry point exists but no page was generated at all should you return to the build side. A single file's import relationships cannot account for those three cases.

### Review Excerpt (Original Meaning Preserved)

"Do not use identically named parameters as proof that their scopes are the same; find the page grouping first, then assess the generator."

This feedback changed the troubleshooting order, but did not provide page samples for every service. It can therefore only serve as an order of operations, not be expanded into a cross-service generation rule.

## Where the Old Links Still Point

The navigation in the old internal record is still:

```text
boto3/docs/client.py
  └─ from botocore.docs.client import ClientDocumenter
```

This navigation is suitable for confirming local files and direct dependencies. It is not suitable for answering how the page is ultimately laid out. After opening the file, if you only see exports or documenter wiring, stop here; do not infer from the file's directory that it is also responsible for the service home page, examples section, or other resource pages.

The card relevant to the current troubleshooting is [SDK-203]. The card is used to return to the verification entry point for the "client context parameters section"; it cannot replace the final service reference page. When comparing them, prioritize saving the original page text and generated file name, so you do not end up with only the terms from the search box.

## 2025-09-18: The Snapshot After the Move to Review

The implementation had already been completed on an existing branch, and the record moved from to-do to review. There is no original issue discussion here to quote verbatim, only this historical action and local path information, so the review action cannot be described as "all pages have been approved". It only indicates that this specific change entered the direct verification phase.

During this verification, three locations are particularly easy to confuse: the body of the service reference page, the group containing regular request members, and the group containing client context parameters. During troubleshooting, write all three on the same sheet of paper, first filling in the headings actually observed, then the links and files. Leave any cell blank if there is no evidence for it.

### If the Page Can Be Opened

1. Search the page body for parameter names related to client initialization.
2. If the search matches regular request members, find that group's heading above them, record the exact text, and do not move the fields.
3. If the search matches a separate heading, record the heading text and its position on the service reference page.
4. If the search only matches navigation or release notes, return to the body and keep looking; proceed to the next branch only if there are still no results in the body.

### If the Page Cannot Be Opened

First distinguish between an old link in a regular directory and permissions for a restricted detail page. The former is a navigation issue, while the latter is an access issue. Neither case directly implies that documentation content is missing. If the generated file can be obtained locally, save its path and the page heading; if only the old link is visible, stop troubleshooting at the link layer.

### If the Source File Can Be Opened

Inspect the local declarations and direct dependencies of `boto3/docs/client.py`. The `ClientDocumenter` in the file header can only serve as an adjacency clue. If you need to confirm the final heading, inspect the generated reference page; do not use this page to expand the responsibilities of `ClientDocumenter` to encompass all service documentation.

## Which Type of Failure to Handle First

You can use the following tree to reconstruct the observed state; its leaves are stopping points, not automatic repair actions:

```text
Problem locating parameters on the reference page
├─ Body is readable
│  ├─ Match in the regular request members group
│  │  ├─ Page also has a client context heading → record the locations of both groups, stop
│  │  └─ No other heading → inspect the generation template, stop at page structure
│  ├─ Only matches navigation or explanatory text → save a copy of the page, check the body again
│  └─ No matches at all → distinguish page generation, links, and permissions
├─ Only an old link is available
│  ├─ Old link in a regular directory → inspect navigation output
│  └─ Restricted detail page permissions → switch to the access entry point, do not change field grouping
└─ Local source file is readable
   ├─ Direct dependencies can be confirmed → record paths and declarations
   └─ Page heading cannot be confirmed → do not fill in conclusions from the path
```

The "Page also has a client context heading" leaf only indicates that the structure can now be located, not that all field content is correct; "No other heading" also only indicates that the generation template needs to be checked again. Do not combine these two assessments into "the documenter is broken".

## Current Verification Entry Point

The service reference output must create a separate Client Context Parameters section for client context parameters, and must not mix these parameters into regular request members.

During verification, first find this heading in the final service reference output, then check whether client context parameters are placed beneath it. Continue inspecting regular request members in their original page group; do not move them together just because their parameter names are similar. If the heading is missing, stop between the generated output and the template, retaining the original page text and the local path for `boto3/docs/client.py`; if the heading exists but the links or fields are incorrect, record discrepancies in the page body and navigation separately.

The current entry point only covers the client context parameters section. It does not answer questions about the directory topology of other service documentation, nor does it cover field definitions for regular request members. If you need to move on to those objects, open a separate record; do not append a generalized conclusion to this tree.

## A Record Format That Remains Usable After Review

Verification of the observed state can be recorded in just four lines:

```text
Page: <Location of the original text on the service reference page>
Regular members group: <Observed heading or empty>
Client context group: <Observed heading or empty>
Next stop: <Body / Template / Navigation / Permissions>
```

The content inside the angle brackets must come from the actual page. If there is no page, write "empty"; do not substitute an expected heading. If returning from [SDK-203], bring back only the navigation for the client context parameters section; do not treat search terms in the card as proof that the page has been generated.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Split Out

This record does not answer how generated files are named, nor does it confirm that all service reference pages use the same navigation hierarchy. The direct dependencies of `boto3/docs/client.py` are sufficient to support tracing back to the entry point, but not to fill these two gaps. If someone later adds page samples, place them in the snapshot section for the corresponding date; do not overwrite the earlier assessments.

Another question can easily get carried along: when the same parameter name appears on different pages, whether all instances belong to client context. The current record only allows judgments based on page headings and parameter groups, and has not established a cross-service list of names. This remains unresolved.

## Old Meeting Appendix: The Simplified Approach Written Down at the Time

The following content is retained, but must no longer be followed:

> First copy the parameters that cannot be found into the regular request parameter list, and organize the headings in the next release. As long as the search returns a match, users will not get stuck.

This reflected a temporary concern about page searchability and had not been checked for scope. Later verification established that being searchable does not mean being correctly placed. If you see this original text on an old page, return to "Current Verification Entry Point" above, and first inspect the separate section and the regular members group.

The meeting margin notes also left a question:

> Is there another template layer between the generator entry point and the final rst file?

The currently frozen materials only establish direct adjacency between `boto3/docs/client.py` and `ClientDocumenter`; there is not enough information to answer this question. Do not use directory names, old links, or a single page search to answer it.

## Stop Conditions

Stop this round of troubleshooting if any of the following occurs: only an old link is available for the page, permissions for the detail page cannot be obtained, the source file can only confirm the entry point but not the generated content, or the page heading and field groups have not both been saved. When stopping, leave the original text you have already seen; do not fill in missing sections just to give the tree a conclusion.

# Batch write retry buffer migration

Let's pin down what we've been discussing. The entry point is still `boto3/dynamodb/table.py`. Previously, we treated "clear the buffer when retries finish" as the migration target. That was too broad: writes arriving during retries would be wiped out too.

Freeze the contents of this round's submission first, then process the unprocessed items. Exclude new writes from this deletion scope; leave them for the next batch request. If review finds that deletion still targets the entire buffer, first revert to the path that deletes only the submission snapshot and stop combined cleanup; don't let a single successful retry hide the loss of later writes.

Additional note: "successfully cleared" does not mean the current buffer object is empty; it only means the data submitted in this round has been processed. A review record that only says "retry succeeded" is not enough to tell whether the migration is correct; also check whether writes arriving during the retry window were retained.

```text
Submission snapshot
  ├─ Unprocessed items → Retry
  └─ Submitted data → Remove after retry succeeds
Newly queued writes → Keep in buffer → Next batch request
```

The diagram shows the boundary to check, not an implementation sequence diagram. Establish the submission snapshot first, and limit removal to that batch of data; even if new writes interleave with retries, leave them for later batch requests. When rolling back, do not restore "clear everything"; retain only the path that can delete within the submission scope.

The initial criterion was simple: if the example section was still visible after opening the maintenance page, the link counted as stable. This criterion was later used to explain the entry point on the service documentation side, making it sound as though the two pages were inherently equivalent.

```text
Before migration
Maintenance page ─────> Example section

After migration (old diagram)
Maintenance page ─────> Example section
Service documentation ────> Example section
```

The problem with the old diagram was not its arrows, but its failure to show the structural differences during page generation. It conflated "the title is visible" with "readers can enter from the expected location". The most recent field feedback disproved this equivalence: even on a page where the title remains visible, the original entry location may not be consistently reproducible. The third step of the old process is therefore no longer sufficient to justify removing the old entry point, but this record has not been retroactively updated into a new general-purpose operating manual.

The verification entry point on the service documentation side is still `boto3/docs/service.py`. The file header exposes very few neighboring objects:

```python
import os
from botocore.docs.bcdoc.restdoc import DocumentStructure
from botocore.docs.service import ServiceDocumenter as BaseServiceDocumenter
from botocore.exceptions import DataNotFoundError
```

Some people initially attributed the issue to `DocumentStructure` on this basis, because it looked like the direct source of the page hierarchy. That judgment is retained here and should no longer be treated as a conclusion about the cause. `DocumentStructure` only shows that structural objects are present during service documentation construction; `BaseServiceDocumenter` indicates that this file is connected near the service documentation base class; `DataNotFoundError` is a reminder that some documentation data may not be retrievable. None of the three can, on its own, explain why entering a given example section from the maintenance page and from the service page leads to different results.

During migration, first record the two pages separately, rather than just noting the four Chinese characters meaning "example section". The maintenance page is where the old entry point resides; the service documentation page is the entry point investigated from the service documentation generation side. Identical titles on the two pages do not mean they come from the same portion of the page structure. The previous record did not distinguish between these, which caused subsequent reviews to switch back and forth between "the link exists" and "navigation is stable".

SDK-209 is the entry point to the card for this record. The card states that Example Section Navigation Stability cannot be consistently reproduced, and calls for identifying the conflicting statements in the two current documents and confirming the maintenance page and the person responsible for updating it. It does not provide an already approved list of new pages, nor does it mean that an explanation was obtained once the toolchain was pinned or work began. The old batch-handling approach can still be used for recovery, but can no longer be used to determine completion:

| Observed situation | Old handling | Significance retained now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The maintenance page provides access to the example section | Keep the entry point | Can serve as a recovery point for readers |
| The service page shows a title with the same name | Consider the migration approved to proceed | Only a page observation |
| The position on the service page differs from that on the old page | Fall back to the old entry point | Still avoids directly deleting a known entry point |
| The two documents make conflicting claims | Choose one to overwrite the other | No longer overwrite either one, first retain the conflicting pages |

Earlier batches left recovery until last: they first tried to replace the maintenance page with the service page, and only added the old link back after readers landed somewhere unexpected. The old instructions recorded only the name "example section", so subsequent reviews could not determine from the name where the old entry point landed on the page. The name can still be used for searching, but it cannot replace the entry point itself.

The value of the maintenance page entry point was also overstated. It is a known fallback location, not a copy of the generated service documentation. The value of the service page entry point was similarly overstated. It provides a verification location on the service documentation side, not evidence that the maintenance page has been synchronized. Both overstatements came from the symmetrical layout of the old diagram: the same title at the ends of two arrows was taken to mean that the work was complete.

# Classic Transport Diagnostic Context Decision Record

During the compatibility train, investigation records for classic transport were gathered at `boto3/s3/transfer.py` under issue names and call names. This entry point is useful for starting checks, but is not a substitute for an explanation of implementation ownership or call coverage. The decision recorded here is for diagnostics to describe the local state at the time of a transport selection, rather than pack subsequent failures, retries, and caller assumptions into the same output entry.

## Decision

The diagnostic context for the classic transport path is to be based on facts that can be established near the transport selection point. At a minimum, log readers must be able to distinguish between the two states `client` and `instance`. The former refers to the client path intended for this transfer; the latter refers to the instance-side state that affects that choice. Both can appear in the same diagnostic output, but neither can be inferred from the other, and neither field can substitute for the other.

This decision defines only the boundaries of the diagnostic context. It does not change the selection made for a transport request, turn logs into a new configuration interface, or require callers to branch on log text. When a compatibility issue arises, first reconstruct the conditions before selection from this context, then return to `boto3/s3/transfer.py` to check whether those conditions still originate in the same place.

## Approaches Considered in Review

**Retain only the client name.** This option is concise, but an investigation would not be able to establish whether instance conditions affected the client selection. A reader could interpret the same client name as implying the same runtime preconditions, then compare results across different instance states. This option was not adopted.

**Assemble complete request information at higher-level call sites.** This appears to offer more clues, but the higher layer sees the request's intent, not necessarily the state when the transport module actually makes its choice. It would also spread the diagnostic format across multiple call entry points, preventing reliable trace-back from old records. This option was not adopted.

**Keep a compact context close to the transport module.** This option keeps the record close to where the choice is made, while limiting its scope to classic transport itself. It does not promise to cover all call parameters or try to explain every exception; when the logs are insufficient to make a determination, the corresponding calls and implementation still need to be examined. This is the option adopted here.

## Boundaries

"Classic transport" is the subject of diagnosis here, not a comparative assessment of other transport implementations. In a record, `client` describes only the choice made on that occasion; it does not mean that a given client is permanently available. `instance` describes only the instance-side state considered during selection, not the instance's full configuration. The two are recorded side by side to avoid reducing a choice to a single name.

Do not add request content, batch parameters, retry buffers, or caller-defined tags to this context. They may affect how an operation appears, but are outside the set of observations this decision is meant to standardize. If these details are gradually appended to transport logs, compatibility investigations will once again depend on each caller's format, and the original entry point will lose its purpose.

Do not gate context output on whether an exception occurs, either. Diagnostics are valuable because they allow comparison of selection conditions in successful and failed cases; adding information only on error paths would leave normal samples unusable as controls. The specific output level and existing logging switches remain governed by the module's existing behavior; this record does not define separate switches.

## Rules for Tracing Back

Investigation records should begin with three questions: which type of `client` was selected at the time; what `instance` state was recorded alongside that choice; and where the two were assembled into the diagnostic context. The first code entry point for the third question is `boto3/s3/transfer.py`.

If an issue name in an old record still points to this file, but the corresponding selection point cannot be found in the code, do not continue extrapolating from the filename. First confirm whether the call name in the old record matches the transport entry point in that version, then decide whether the investigation needs to continue through adjacent calls. This preserves the usefulness of the old investigation entry point without mistaking it for a permanent description of the call chain.

The review explicitly rejected another formulation: collapsing client selection, instance conditions, and the final transport result into a single "fell back" or "matched" statement. Such a summary seemed easy to read at the time, but dropped the preconditions that most needed to be compared. When selections differ, keep the preconditions and the result separate; only state that can be confirmed near the module belongs in this diagnostic context.

## Impact on the Compatibility Train

Checks within the train should treat this record as a guide to the order of investigation, not as a pass criterion. If the logs distinguish `client` from `instance`, that shows the classic transport diagnostic view is still available; additions, deletions, or reordering of the log text alone do not establish that transport behavior has changed. Conversely, even if the transport result is as expected, conflating the two pre-selection states into a single concept will still leave subsequent investigations without comparable samples.

This also constrains how review questions are phrased. You can ask, "What was the instance state when this client was selected?" You should not directly ask, "Which client is this instance guaranteed to use?" The first question refers to an actual selection; the second misrepresents a dynamic decision as a static promise, making it easy to misdiagnose environmental differences as compatibility regressions.

This decision is retained not to add explanatory text to the transport module, but to let old records, code entry points, and new diagnostic samples use the same set of local concepts. If the diagnostic scope genuinely needs to expand later, specify separately whether the newly added state comes from before, during, or after selection; do not change the meaning of the existing `client` and `instance` fields.

Whether all call entry points can provide the same instance-side information has not yet been covered here. Log formatting cannot settle that question; when a specific gap appears, it needs to be verified separately by following the actual call relationships.
