# Proposal for Unknown API Version Errors

This interface review did not start with "whether to add another exception type", but instead first examined two distinct failure entry points in the resource model. In one, the resource name has been found, but the requested API version is outside that resource's supported range; in the other, the resource model itself could not be resolved. Both may look like loading failures to callers, but they are not the same thing for troubleshooting: the former should identify the requested version and provide the versions allowed for this resource; the latter has no basis for pretending to know the version set.

The early draft combined these two entry points because the call sites were close together. That judgment is no longer being used. Proximity does not mean they can share an error contract; if the model has not been established, an assembled list of "available versions" would only disguise missing information as a result. The old draft is retained in the previous version to explain why centralized assembly was discussed first at the time, not because that path is still a valid basis for implementation.

## What this round needs to pin down

The discussion is limited to requests for a resource's API version. The resource name is part of the externally exposed error, so retaining only an internal lookup key is not enough; the requested version must not be lost during exception propagation either. The version set represents the currently known supported range for that resource and should be expressed separately from cases such as "the model does not exist".

`boto3/resources/model.py` remains the starting point for tracing back. The visible `xform_name` indicates that resource name conversion is an adjacent step requiring particular attention: the review should confirm whether the error uses the caller-facing resource name or a name used only for internal model lookup. We do not assume that the two are the same, nor do we require an additional conversion just for the error text. If the existing path already produces a stable resource name before the version check, reuse it; if not, perform the conversion at an explicit boundary rather than leaving each call site to handle it independently.

The `logging` in the file should likewise not become part of the error contract. Logs can help identify the branches taken during resource model loading, but callers depend on the information carried by the exception, not on a particular debug output. Relying on logs for the version, resource name, and version set would prevent normal call paths from making the same determination and would also make behavior uncertain when logging is disabled or the log level is adjusted.

## Two implementation approaches

The first approach is to throw only a narrowly scoped unsupported-version signal at the model layer. After receiving the signal, the higher layer retrieves the resource name, requested version, and supported set to assemble the externally exposed exception. The benefit is that the model layer takes on less responsibility for presentation formatting; the cost is that the higher layer must retrieve all three pieces of information again. If the resource name undergoes conversion, the call site also has to know when that conversion happens. Different entry points could easily produce slightly different text later, especially when the version list is empty, its order differs, or name normalization is incomplete.

The second approach is to create a dedicated exception at the check where the resource name, requested version, and supported set are already available together, then propagate it along the existing resource-loading path. This does not mean using the exception to replace all model errors, but rather encapsulating "the resource exists, but the requested version is unsupported" separately. The advantage is that all three pieces of information come from the same check; the disadvantage is that we must confirm that the check really covers only this meaning and does not misclassify model parsing failures, missing service definitions, or other loading problems as unsupported versions.

For this round, we recommend trying the second approach. It differs from the initial draft in that: the initial draft considered having an arbitrary higher layer add the message text centrally; now, the exception may only be created where the complete version-check context is already available. The exception's contents should remain stable and, at a minimum, let callers identify the resource, the rejected version, and the set of allowed versions. That version set is neither a general SDK support table nor a default borrowed from another resource.

## Document the counterexamples alongside the proposal first

An unsupported version is not the same as having no version. If a resource has only one available version, the error should still list that single-element set; it must not switch to a different summary description just because the list is short. Conversely, if the resource model never loaded successfully, do not construct an empty set and classify the failure as an unsupported version. An empty set would mislead callers into thinking that the resource model had been identified but currently had no compatible versions.

The resource name should not be freely guessed by the layer reporting the error either. If the name passed by the caller has a different form from the name in the model, first follow the existing path to confirm which one is the public resource name. Putting the raw input directly into the error could expose an internal key that has never appeared in the resource documentation; forcing the normalized result back onto every entry point could change lookup logic that did not need to change. This proposal only requires using the resource identifier already accepted by that path when the version check is complete.

There is another easily overlooked branch: the caller Fang Ke may only want to probe whether a version is available, with no intention of continuing to construct a resource object. If such probes share the version check with normal construction, their callers should be able to recognize the dedicated exception; if a probe bypasses the resource model, it must not be forced back into the full construction flow merely to make the text uniform. The review aims to stabilize the error boundary, not rearrange every entry point for resource loading.

## Arranging the regression cases

SDK-212 can serve as navigation entry points for this round of regression testing. The cases should closely follow the current resource model path, without substituting server responses or network behavior for local version checks. The minimum set includes: a known resource with an unsupported version, the same resource with a supported version, and the existing failure path when the resource model does not exist. The first two confirm that the version gate does not swallow request information, while the third confirms that the new logic has not expanded to cover non-version issues.

We do not recommend designing these cases as an enumeration of every combination of all resources and all versions. Version lists come from the individual resource models, and repeating the same check does not increase confidence in the interface. It is more useful to choose an object with an easy-to-read supported set and a resource name processed through the normal path, then observe whether all three required pieces of information are already available where the exception is created. If the cases have to assemble resource names or version sets separately in multiple higher layers, the boundary for the second approach has been chosen too late, and we should stop and locate the version check again rather than copy formatting code just to get the tests to pass first.

The version list must retain the order provided by the existing model when presented. No new sorting rule is being introduced here; sorting specifically for the error message would mix a data representation change into the exception contract and obscure whether the model itself is stable. If the existing collection does not have a predictable order, first confirm where it comes from in the model, then decide what the regression tests should pin down rather than compensating at the message layer.

## Corrections in the review record

The subsequent review record noted that one point in this contract remains unconfirmed, pending another check through the same entry point. We therefore cannot currently conclude that "the exception is already produced consistently across all resource paths". What can already be retained is the proposal's boundary: unsupported versions and missing models are kept separate; the dedicated exception is created only where the resource, requested version, and available versions are all known; higher layers do not reassemble these three items.

Two items remain to be confirmed. First, whether the precise point at which the resource name goes through `xform_name` precedes the version check; this determines which form of the name the regression tests should compare, rather than requiring a change to name handling. Second, whether the supported version set in this branch comes from the same model object; if it comes from a later query, the exception may still be created too early. The follow-up review should record these two points as actual observations, not replace them with "they appear to be at the same layer".

Quality checks should not abandon the entire regression entry point because of these two open questions. For now, we can decline to extend this contract to other resource-loading exceptions while retaining the local cases and existing failure paths. This way, if the second check shows that the name or version set comes from different stages, the scope of the changes will remain at the check boundary rather than affecting all resource model callers.

## Withdrawal conditions

Withdraw the current second approach if any of the following occurs:

- The public resource name is unavailable at the version check, leaving only higher-layer guesswork or repeated conversion;
- The set of allowed versions is not information directly available from that resource model and can only be obtained by crossing another failure boundary;
- Throwing the dedicated exception requires rewriting existing errors, such as a missing model or parsing failure, as version errors;
- The normal and unknown versions of the same resource take different model-selection paths in the cases, so the so-called "available versions" do not come from the same object.

Withdrawal does not mean returning to assembly at an arbitrary higher layer as in the initial draft. At that point, first record the information already available at each entry point, then decide whether an internal signal carrying only structured fields is needed, or whether to retain the existing errors and defer the interface contract. Until this step is complete, do not promise that the error text will be exactly the same across all paths.

The deliverables of this proposal are an identifiable unsupported-version boundary and adjacent regression cases, not a comprehensive rewrite of the resource model error system. SDK-212 remain entry points for the regression records; for runtime issues involving instance optimization and the order of version gating, see DOC-23 separately to avoid conflating the two kinds of version semantics into a single change.

# Transport Instance Optimization Troubleshooting Procedure

Notes on a set of inconsistent transport behaviors in 2026.09 Compatibility Train: both success and failure had been observed for the same type of call. In the discussion, the difference was initially attributed to the order of instance optimization and version gating. The old troubleshooting entry point is `boto3/s3/transfer.py`.

The working hypothesis at the time was that the instance optimization decision first determined the transport-side candidates, and the version gate then filtered out ineligible candidates. This hypothesis helped explain some of the failure records, but no material was available yet for comparing the two outcomes under the same conditions.

```text
Call outcomes differ
├─ Instance optimization state is known
│  ├─ Yes: first record the candidate client and the version check that follows
│  └─ No: do not label the failure directly as a version incompatibility
└─ Instance optimization state was not recorded
   ├─ Review the inputs used when creating TransferConfig
   └─ Still unable to fill in the gaps: leave unclassified; do not infer the order
```

The old notes required "instance optimization state," "preferred client," and "where the version check appeared" to be captured in the same annotation. Only use the order above if the records show that the version check occurred after the candidates were determined. If only the final exception remains in the record, stop at the call site; do not reconstruct the intermediate path from the exception name.

It is easy to conflate instance optimization with a successful call, but they are not synonymous. A successful result only shows that the call did not hit the recorded failure surface; it does not, by itself, prove that the version gate had been passed. Conversely, a failure alone does not prove that instance optimization was involved in selection.

Pending review: was the version check in the failed call generated during transport configuration, or did it only become visible during the subsequent client selection stage?

# Transfer Instance Optimization Troubleshooting Workflow

This page is still retained as the legacy troubleshooting entry point used during the compatibility train. The earliest records placed successful and failed calls side by side, and the only consistently identifiable distinction was the repeated mention of "instance optimization" and "version gating" in the discussions. These two terms were not separated at the time, so different people assigned the same exception to different branches.

The old entry point has always been listed as `boto3/s3/transfer.py`. It is useful for tracing back from transfer objects, but that does not mean every failure is determined in this file. The initial draft overstated this: it suggested that simply finding `TransferConfig` would let you reconstruct the call's entire selection process. That claim was later crossed out; it is retained here because many old links still lead through this entry point.

## The Tree Left by the Initial Draft

The tree below shows the sequence actually used at the time. It puts instance optimization first and treats the version gate as the next checkpoint. It is not a post-review explanation of the sequence.

```text
Both successful and failed call outcomes occur
│
├─ Can the instance optimization state be identified?
│  │
│  ├─ Yes
│  │  ├─ State is enabled
│  │  │  ├─ Record the preferred client
│  │  │  ├─ Record whether CRT appears
│  │  │  └─ Then look for text left by the version gate
│  │  │
│  │  └─ State is not enabled
│  │     ├─ Do not attribute the failure directly to the version
│  │     └─ Look back at the inputs recorded when the transfer configuration was created
│  │
│  └─ No
│     ├─ Save only the call outcome and existing exception text
│     ├─ Do not infer the state from the final outcome
│     └─ Stop classifying
│
└─ Has a version check already been seen?
   ├─ Yes: The old workflow assumes it occurs after the candidate is determined
   └─ No: The old workflow does not allow "version check passed" to be entered
```

This tree had an assumption that was not written down at the time: the "state" in a record must come from material associated with that same call. Splicing in results from another machine, another configuration set, or a later retry can make the tree appear navigable without establishing the order. During the later review, this kind of splicing was the most common problem; a successful-call record was used to fill in the missing state in a failed-call record, ultimately leading to the conclusion that "instance optimization bypassed the gate".

That conclusion is no longer accepted. Success only shows that the call reached an outcome that did not fail; failure only shows that the call in the other record was blocked somewhere. The two can suggest what should be compared, but cannot by themselves establish the sequence within a call.

## What to Do First After the Review

First, separate the material by call. Do not start by labeling calls as taking the "CRT path" or the "classic path". For each call, write down only what was actually recorded: whether `TransferConfig` can be seen near the transfer configuration, whether the preferred client was recorded, whether the instance optimization state has a clear source, and exactly where the version-gate text appears. If any item is missing, leave it missing.

`preferred_transfer_client` is an object name worth copying down separately during troubleshooting, but it is not a substitute field for the instance optimization state. Old records interpreted "the preferred client has been determined" as "instance optimization has taken effect". That step was unsupported: preference, availability, and instance optimization are three distinct aspects to evaluate. When recording them, do not combine them under an umbrella label such as "selected transfer mode".

Similarly, `HAS_CRT` can only help establish whether the availability of CRT was factored into the assessment at the time. It cannot replace evidence of the version gate. The version gate concerns whether a candidate meets the version requirements in effect at the time; availability is a separate question. The old page squeezed these two checks onto one line, so some people saw that CRT was available and wrote "the gate should pass", while others saw the gate fail and wrote "CRT is unavailable". Both of these additions should be removed from the records, rather than rewritten as smoother explanations.

It is recommended to organize a call into the following four lines, which do not all have to be complete:

```text
Call identifier: Include only the part of the existing logs or test records that distinguishes this call
Near the configuration: TransferConfig / Not recorded
Instance optimization: Explicitly enabled, explicitly not enabled, or not recorded
Client and version: Excerpt them separately, without inferring either one from the other
```

If all that remains under "Near the configuration" is the entry point for `boto3/s3/transfer.py`, do not fill in parameter values for it. The path can help the next troubleshooter find the local object, but cannot recover the actual inputs to that call.

## Branch 1: Only the Final Exception Is Available When the Failure Occurs

This is the situation in which the old workflow is most likely to mislead. First, check whether the instance optimization state is directly recorded near the exception. If not, do not enter either the "enabled" or "not enabled" subtree. The old version treated this blank as "usually not enabled", on the grounds that the failed call left no text about an available client; that rationale has been discarded.

Next, look for a version check recorded as separate text. If it appears, record where it appears, but do not write "the gate comes after instance optimization". The position is only its position within the material, unless the same record explicitly shows the call relationships between the checks. If there is no separate version-related text, stop at "failure cause not yet classified".

The stopping condition is simple: when there is only a final exception, with no state or configuration excerpt from the same call, make no further sequence-based attributions. You may retain the original exception text and entry-point path, but must not fill the failure description with speculation. This stopping point preserves room for later comparisons, not to suggest that the failure is unimportant.

## Branch 2: A Successful Call Is Used for Comparison

Use successful-call records first to rule out obvious differences in what was recorded, not to prove how the failed call made its internal selections. When comparing, ask only three questions: does each record contain the instance optimization state; does each contain client-related text; does each have an independent trace of the version gate. If any item exists only on the successful side, it can only be marked "missing on the failed side".

The old approach was to take an apparently normal sequence from a successful call and apply it to the failed call. This expands "the successful call did not trigger a failure" into "the failed call must have failed at the same stage". This approach is no longer used after the review. Successful-call records still have value: they remind troubleshooters not to collapse the preferred client, CRT availability, and instance optimization into a single Boolean result, and they also remind people to list the version gate separately.

When there is enough material on both sides, use cautious wording to record the comparison, such as "the successful side recorded the client and the instance optimization state; the failed side recorded only version-related text". Do not reduce this statement to "version precedes optimization" or "optimization bypasses the version check". The former describes the internal order, while the latter describes the mechanism's effect, and neither is confirmed by the available records.

## Branch 3: A Transfer Configuration Object Is Visible

After seeing `TransferConfig`, pause. It is a place to verify configuration inputs, not evidence that a check has already run. The old notes treated it as a master switch: whenever a configuration object appeared, they assumed instance optimization, client selection, and version gating would all complete in a set order. The review did not support this extrapolation.

Three types of information should be recorded separately here:

- Whether inputs related to transfer selection explicitly appear in the configuration;
- Whether the same call recorded the instance optimization state;
- Whether the version gate appears near the configuration, near client selection, or only at the final exception.

If the first item is present but the other two are not, this only shows that troubleshooting has located a configuration object. Do not rewrite "a configuration exists" as "a particular client was used", and do not write "the version check is complete". If the third item comes only from another call, return to Branch 2 rather than filling in the gaps across calls.

This paragraph was added later because the old troubleshooting approach kept expanding the scope of reading along the path, eventually mixing findings from reading the code with records of a single failure. You can still follow this path to inspect local objects, but the failure notes must identify which statements come from call records and which are merely assessments made during troubleshooting. Without material attributable to the call, the latter should not become conclusions.

## Old Recovery Actions and Their Problems

Early on, some people suggested treating instance optimization as not enabled whenever a failure occurred, then checking the version gate. The benefit of this action is that it quickly moves the tree into a branch, but the downside is that it overwrites the original blank: later readers cannot tell whether the state was never recorded or was actually observed as not enabled.

Another action was to fall back to a "classic transfer" explanation whenever traces related to CRT appeared. This is also retained on the old page because the on-call records from that time show searches in that direction; but it did not resolve the sequencing issue. Classic Transport Diagnostic Context, automatic transfer manager fallback, and version gating are not the same check. Calling all of them "fallback" broadens the failure surface without adding a single piece of comparable evidence.

Neither action is recommended any longer as an attribution step. If an old ticket has already used one of them, retain the original wording and add "state filled in based on speculation" or "client and version checks conflated" alongside it. Do not silently change it to a new conclusion, or subsequent readers will not be able to understand why the old records reached different answers.

## What to Leave in the Handoff

This page deals only with the relationship between instance optimization and version gating. When handing the material over, include the raw output excerpt from the same call, any known information near `TransferConfig`, and the three separately recorded states for instance optimization, client, and version. If no raw excerpt is available, the handoff text should state directly "final exception only".

If the issue shifts to exhaustion of waiter checks, do not continue to reuse the transfer branches here; waiter semantics are covered separately in DOC-24. Conversely, when you see a transfer failure, do not merge content from the waiter page into this page just to fill out the record.

What remains unconfirmed is whether, in a reproducible failed call, a single record can clearly establish the order of the version check and the instance optimization check. The old tree once gave an affirmative answer, but after the review this can only remain an open item for further investigation.

# Current and Legacy Entry Point Migration Index

This index is kept in boto3 · Client Integration's migration directory. It records the legacy entry points still used by `boto3-client-integration`, their replacement locations, and the boundaries encountered during integration. Objects are registered based only on actual call samples; pages with the same name in the directory do not necessarily belong to the same migration path.

## Migration Order

First, capture the entry point name and request object the caller is using, then check the replacement location in `docs/adj-boto3/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Switch the call to the current entry point only after verification passes. During the switch, retain the original call's parameters and failure output, especially at `RequestItems`; this was once used to assess whether the two entry-point paths could be merged directly, and was later retained as a reference point for tracing back.

"Current entry point" in the directory means only the location intended for use when this page was written. It does not mean all callers have completed migration. The callers using `account_id` at the time were not recorded; a new name appearing in the directory is not a substitute for confirmation. Migration completion still needs to be confirmed with each actual consumer, not inferred from the new entry point's presence in the directory.

## Earlier Assessment and Recovery

An earlier comparison looked at continuing through `ServiceDocumenter` versus splitting `UnknownAPIVersionError` out on its own. The old notes favored the latter because the two segments appeared to have different failure exits. If a caller encounters a failure exit after the switch that was not there before, first stop at the current entry point and save the request object and corresponding output, then restore the legacy entry point that caller previously used. # LICENSE Entry Point Migration Index

Entry points in the documentation site cannot all be replaced in one pass based on directory names. Old entry points often carry both version notes and outdated-content warnings; if only the links to the new locations are updated, consumers still entering through old records will see mixed content. Start verification at `docs/adj-license/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`; each item in the index corresponds to just one old entry point, one replacement location, and the known consumers.

## How to Record Migrations

1. First, retain the original location of the old entry point; don't use similarly named pages to fill in missing items. Record the version notes it carries and its existing outdated status beside the old entry point.
2. Register the replacement location in the same item. The replacement location is a path that lets consumers continue into the documentation site; it is not equivalent to a newly created page in the directory.
3. List known consumers separately after the old entry point. To verify an item, follow the path from the consumer's original record to the current revision; if the path cannot be followed, record where it fails and do not count the item as migrated.
4. Keep notes that cannot be traced back marked as outdated. Do not delete the old notes or mark them as migrated just because the replacement location already exists.

Track old entry points, new entry points, and compatible callers separately. This allows a link in the same migration batch to have moved to its replacement location while another consumer remains on the old path; neither state overrides the other.

## Completion Criteria and Recovery

To consider a migration complete, actual consumers must be able to reach the replacement location from their original records and read the corresponding version notes. Seeing the current entry point only in the directory or a report is not enough to close the old entry point. When index timestamps and documentation page timestamps differ, leave the time difference in place; don't use a page written later to explain an earlier record.

If a replacement location cannot support a known consumer, restore the old entry point for that item: make the old location an accessible path again, retain its outdated-content warning, and set the replacement location back to pending verification. Restore only this entry point; do not roll back other items in the batch that have already been verified.

The documentation site has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. An index item must not be delivered as complete before consumer verification; a change of maintainer cannot replace that step either. Still missing: the active callers of `contextParams`, and whether only the old entry point is restored on withdrawal.

The break was first recorded when a user was following the path from the current entry point toward the current revision. Not enough page content was saved to put a page name to the stopping point. If material preserves only the entry point and none of the subsequent pages, it only shows that the observation stopped after the entry point.

I'd previously remembered "being able to continue from the same entry point once" as almost meaning recovery. Checking the old records later showed that wasn't right: the visible results didn't fully match, and the other user path hadn't come back. In particular, the result showing that one path could continue must not be reassigned to the other path. There is no saved content to confirm whether both went through the same turning point.

# license-portal Maintainer Map

The earliest surviving artifact was a three-row table. `Session` was listed as "Module on-call," `Sphinx` said "Not yet confirmed," and `awscrt` said "Caller to add name." Putting these terms in the same table left the boundaries between page maintenance, temporary handoffs, and technical assessments unclear. The old table is retained, but it cannot be used directly as the present contact list.

For requests coming in through `docs/adj-license/ownership/license-documentation-portal-current-maintainer-map.md`, first identify what kind of item the request concerns. Page text, attachments, and release notes go through LICENSE · User Documentation Portal's maintenance entry point; retirement actions use the on-call entry point instead. When shared interfaces or the behavior of the SDK module need assessment, this table does not answer on the module owner's behalf.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User or maintenance request] --> P[license-documentation-portal]
    P --> W[Pages, attachments, release notes]
    P --> E[Retirement actions]
    P --> T[Module technical assessment]
    W --> M[LICENSE · User Documentation Portal maintenance entry point]
    E --> D[adj-license on-call entry point]
    T --> O[Relevant module owner]
    D --> H[Unfilled temporary assignee slot]
```

| Item involved | First point of contact | Can handle | Judgments it cannot replace |
|---|---|---|---|
| `license-documentation-portal` pages and attachments | Wu Tong (`peer-03`) | Entry-point text, page materials, release notes, flagging and handing off outdated content | Long-term technical conclusions about SDK or shared interfaces |
| Retirement actions | `adj-license` on-call entry point | Record the entry point to retire, retain old records, confirm whether migration is needed | Having the page maintainer decide the timing of technical deletion |
| Temporary handoff | On-call entry point; specific name not yet filled in | Take the request, retain the original input, page version, and first visible result | Registering the temporary assignee as the long-term owner |
| Module behavior or implementation issues | Relevant module owner | Once the item is identified, hand over the original question and the minimal observed behavior | Having the page maintainer reach a conclusion based on the entry-point name |
| Page relationships requiring review | Migration materials for `DOC-31` | Cross-check records of entry points and retirement actions | Rewriting migration records as a responsibility table |

"Temporary assignee" is not another name for "current maintainer." The assignee's job is to get the request and source materials to whoever can assess them, not to reach a conclusion on behalf of an absent owner. If the request already falls outside page maintenance, stop at the entry point for the relevant module owner. The old table did not spell out this distinction, so it combined page issues, module issues, and temporary actions taken when no one was available.

On 1/20, an observed discrepancy was noted alongside the record for `SDKB-007`: the two environments had different "current results," and the command had not yet been found. This only shows that entry-point verification was incomplete; it is not grounds for naming a new long-term owner. In similar cases, record the pages, release notes, or attachments seen in each of the two environments separately. Do not merge entry points with similar names into one. That card's task is to record the source and the party using each of the two "current entry points." It is useful for explaining why the table needs to be split, but cannot be used to fill in a personnel list.

`SDKB-010` later moved into outdated-navigation cleanup. The recorded blocker was "the LICENSE · User Documentation Portal Core Module on-call person is out today." This shows that the on-call entry point may temporarily have no one available to take requests; it does not mean that the most recently contacted person automatically becomes the owner. When cleaning up outdated navigation, first retain the original "license-documentation-portal Current Maintainer Map" record and its date, then log the retirement action through the on-call entry point. Page content and module technical assessments must still be handled separately.

### Retained Items from the Old Table

The following three items reflect the work as it stood at an earlier point in time and are no longer used as a complete mapping:

- `Session`: The original table only said "Module on-call," without distinguishing between page maintenance and module assessments.
- `Sphinx`: The original table said "Not yet confirmed"; no name has been filled in on this page.
- `awscrt`: The original table said "Caller to add name." This means the handoff item was incomplete, not that the caller was responsible for page maintenance.

The specific name of the temporary assignee when the on-call person is absent is still blank. The latest reply should not be used to fill that blank. To handle pages, attachments, or outdated navigation, start at the `adj-license` entry point. # notice-supply-boundary Maintainer Map

The entry point is still at `docs/adj-notice/ownership/notice-supply-boundary-current-maintainer-map.md`. It started as a small table for finding contacts. It has since been cited more often, but that does not make it a definitive reference for every object.

Of the three names recorded in v1, `Sphinx` is the module on-call entry point, `RequestItems` requires the caller to supply a name, and `awscrt` has no long-term contact. The gaps in the last two entries mean different things: the former is missing adopter information, while the latter is missing maintenance ownership. Labeling both "To be confirmed" would cause someone taking over temporarily to use the wrong material.

The old table's "module on-call" label is now too broad. It applies only to regular directory links and page-generation locations at the entry-point layer. It cannot be extended to `BatchWriter` behavior, the licensing scope of `RequestItems`, or any question not yet tied to an object. The row is retained to make the old handoff records understandable; for new questions, do not just write "contact module on-call".

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Received a notice-supply-boundary question] --> P{Where does the question land first?}
    P -->|Entry point or broken link| N[NOTICE · Dependency Boundary Audit on-call contact]
    P -->|BatchWriter behavior or artifacts| B[Module maintainer]
    P -->|RequestItems scope or licensing| R[Relevant decision-maker]
    P -->|UnprocessedItems or awscrt| U[Keep the slot open and take over temporarily]
    N --> X[Hand over the original link, time, and minimal observed behavior]
    B --> X
    R --> X
    U --> X
    X --> E[Document the exit action]
```

| Object or destination | First point of contact | Material to provide | Responsibility ends here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project entry point, old links for regular directories | NOTICE · Dependency Boundary Audit on-call contact | Link location, original page status, minimal observed behavior | The on-call contact confirms the entry point or passes the material to the object's maintainer |
| `BatchWriter` behavior, generated artifacts, or anomalies | Module maintainer | Object name, where it is used, first visible result | The module maintainer assesses only that object and does not explain scope on the adopter's behalf |
| `RequestItems` risk, licensing, or adoption scope | Relevant decision-maker | The name and scope question supplied by the caller | The decision-maker does not fill in implementation details for the implementer |
| `UnprocessedItems` | No long-term maintainer; a temporary assignee holds the material | Original input, entry point, handoff time, contacts already tried | Do not fill in the official owner field before confirmation |
| `awscrt` | No long-term maintainer; a temporary assignee holds the material | Where it was found and the specific object that needs assessment | Do not infer ownership from an adjacent module or whoever replied most recently |

"Taking over temporarily" here is not a new long-term role. It covers only three things: accepting material with no owner, breaking questions back down to the object level, and documenting when to exit. If an object later has a clear maintainer, just append a line identifying the new point of contact; do not erase the old vacancy, or past handoffs will look as though they were left out of the record.

One old handling practice should also be called out: someone once put `BatchWriter` and `RequestItems` in the same handoff because both appeared in the same user's description. That practice no longer applies. `BatchWriter` behavior and artifacts go to the module maintainer, while `RequestItems` risk, licensing, or scope goes to the relevant decision-maker; the user only needs to fill in the objects and scope they observed.

The record for SDKC-005 reminds us that revision status remains unknown until it has been confirmed whether collection or execution took place. "Handed off" therefore must not be recorded as "verified". The approach used for SDKC-007 was to keep the old assessment in place and append the later NOTICE · Dependency Boundary Audit results; this page follows that approach and has not filled v1's vacant slots to make the list look tidier in hindsight.

DOC-35 can still serve as an entry point to the original context of the first broken link. If the problem starts with a broken link, hand it first to the NOTICE · Dependency Boundary Audit on-call contact; if the material already clearly points to `BatchWriter`, `RequestItems`, `UnprocessedItems`, or `awscrt`, route it directly by object using the table. This routing split is the last part of the old diagram still worth keeping.

# Compatibility Catalog Window Closeout Checklist

This checklist keeps the original window scope: borrow the current entry point, retain the final output, record the return time, and use the rollback entry point when needed. It is not the complete release process for the Resource Models and Exceptions compatibility catalog. Catalog maintenance, migration records, and caller compatibility remain in their original locations; this records what must still be visible as the window is about to end.

The old version treated the entry point being openable and the output being retained as conditions for closing the window, and allowed the handoff signature for the exit action to be added later. That rule remains in v1; it was not removed. The handoff time added later is present, but the handoff signature for the exit entry is still blank. Recording a handoff time does not mean someone has taken over the exit action; the old checklist did not distinguish these two things at the time.

Before closing the window, process the items below in order. Each item records only the entry point actually borrowed for this window and its result; it does not turn objects seen during local troubleshooting into catalog state.

1. **Pin down the entry point first.** Open `docs/adj-resource-model/release/resource-models-and-exceptions-compatibility-catalog-pre-window-close-checklist.md`. Before starting, note the current entry point, borrowed item, planned return time, and first visible result. Leaving the entry-point name by itself is not useful; subsequent output must make clear that it belongs to this window. If the borrowed item can no longer be identified, do not fill in "returned" yet.

2. **Keep two samples.** The current entry point must retain one success path and one rejection path. The rejection path is not there just to pad the test record; it prevents a situation where, after only green output remains, we can no longer tell whether the entry point still behaves within its original boundary. Recheck the public entry point using the original `resource-model-compatibility-catalog` once more; the local result is diagnostic material only and cannot replace this recheck. If the public entry point is unavailable, stop at this item; do not use local output to close out the window.

3. **Record diagnostic changes to the live state separately.** Results obtained after changing the state for troubleshooting must be kept separate from the original window output. Do not overwrite the original failure or rejection with a cleaned-up successful result. A restored result may be appended alongside the original record, but it should not replace the last original output; otherwise later readers will see only the restored state and not why the window was not closed at the time.

4. **Treat the exit action as a separate check.** Before the deadline, contact the person originally responsible to confirm the exit entry point. If there is no reply, still close out using the existing exit action, but the status may only be written as handoff unconfirmed; it cannot be marked complete just because a handoff time has been recorded. Check the final output, return time, and handoff signature in the same place; if any one is blank, keep the window open or explicitly leave it incomplete.

5. **Keep the old route before rolling back.** If a rollback is needed, first delete the route pointing to the old exit action and retain the pre-change route snapshot, then close out using the existing exit action. The records SDKD-001 document exactly this step: the route for the old exit action must not be erased directly without a snapshot. Here, "rollback" refers only to handling the exit for the current entry point; it does not mean rolling back the other changes to the compatibility catalog as well.

Closing the window does not make this page a final conclusion. SDKD-002 require the restored result to be kept alongside the original state; SDKD-009 require rechecking through the public entry point, with the local result still used only for diagnosis. The checkpoint in SDKD-010 is to contact the person originally responsible before the exit action expires. SDKD-011 leave a follow-up judgment: recheck the current revision during the first complete window after closing; if it is still abnormal, reopen the current entry point and reconnect it to the original timeline.

### Stop and Roll Back

- The final output was not retained: stop; do not close the window just because the entry point can still be opened.
- The return time is not specified: stop; the borrowed item remains in the window.
- The public entry point's result differs from the local diagnostic result: stop; retain both results side by side and do not choose one as the conclusion.
- If the handoff signature is blank, the existing exit action may still be used to close out, but mark the window as incomplete; do not write it as handed off.
- If a rollback is needed, retain the old route snapshot first; if the snapshot is missing, do not delete the route.

The old version's "add the signature later" convention can still be used to understand why the window was closed at the time, but it cannot be used to override the blank signature that remains now. The restoration recheck in the public environment has not yet been written into this record; until it appears, the green result after restoration only indicates one check performed after restoration, not that the original window has been fully confirmed.

# Session Credential Failure On-Call Page

This revision still treats this as a single failed run; do not fold in other alerts from the same time period. After receiving the alert, first save the raw page state, original input, current version, and first result. Even if the page later turns green, it must not replace this record.

## What to Preserve First

At the start of the on-call shift, do not restart, refresh credentials, or recreate data for reproduction, unless that action itself is the condition being compared. While the run has not stabilized, first preserve test logs or trace snippets; excerpt only what can identify the location of the first divergence, and do not turn it into a root-cause narrative.

The old record says to look for `deferred logging` first. This entry point is still useful: it lets the person taking over return to the earliest point where a discrepancy appeared. It is not a determination of the cause of failure. After seeing the tag, continue checking the raw state before and after it; if there is no comparison sample, record "no comparison" and do not fill in the gap using another run.

## First Anomaly

`UnprocessedItems` is the earliest stop marker retained on this page. When it appears, leave the page, input, and output at that time unchanged, and write down the preceding item, the item itself, and the following item. Do not clean up before confirming, because a green result left after cleanup cannot show where the original discrepancy was.

The old version says: if `TransferConfig` does not appear, stop here. Reserve this action for handoffs with no other clues; it does not mean that the missing tag itself is the fault, nor that the configuration necessarily changed. If this run's first discrepancy has already appeared at an earlier point, stop at that earlier point; do not jump to `TransferConfig` just to fill out the old form.

## How to Compare

Compare item by item only with the most recent normal sample, changing only one condition at a time. First compare whether the input is the same, then check the version and first result; if these three already differ, do not move on to session or credential speculation. After the comparison, state which condition has not changed and which condition still lacks evidence; do not record "no difference observed" as "verified."

`BatchWriter` and `RequestItems` are to be recorded only as incident-scene labels. The handoff note must preserve the order in which they appeared in the current run; do not infer processing order from their names. ## Handoff

The handoff record must retain at least: the page entry, the first difference, actions not performed, hypotheses that have been ruled out, and where to resume next time. # On-Call Page for a Failed Session and Credentials Run

This page covers a single failed run of session-auth-quality-signal. When on call, first treat it as a record of the observed state, not as an opportunity to rerun it. Preserve the page state already observed, the original input, the version, the first result, and log snippets that locate the first divergence before doing any cleanup. If the page later recovers, do not delete the description of the earlier failure.

## Initial Records

First confirm that you are handling a single run, without mixing in other prompts from the same period. On the record page, write only the objects and sequence you can currently see: where the input appeared, what the first differing result was, and which snippets were saved at the time. If there is no run marker, write "Run marker not retained"; do not fill one in based on the version name, page title, or the incoming operator's memory.

The original procedure was to open `docs/adj-session-auth/runbooks/sessions-and-credentials-quality-signal-board-failed-run-on-call-page.md` first and look for `deferred logging` in the records. Keep this location, because older samples often start to diverge here. It is only an index, not an explanation of the session, credentials, or regression layer. If the earliest difference in this run comes before it, record the earlier location first; the old entry point can remain in the notes.

The default action at the start of the on-call shift is to leave the observed state untouched. Do not restart, refresh credentials, recreate the input, or clean up the page first just to obtain a clean log. These actions may be performed only when the actions themselves are listed as comparison conditions for this run; record the state before the action before performing it. This is not because every refresh causes a problem, but because the result after a refresh cannot replace the first result.

The "most recent normal sample" in the old version can still serve as a starting point, but it is not evidence of success. First compare the inputs, versions, and first results from both sides side by side. If any of the three already differs, do not extend the explanation beyond that difference. If no usable normal sample is available, state that there is no comparison sample; do not take a snippet from another run and use it as a baseline for the same environment.

## When `UnprocessedItems` Appears

`UnprocessedItems` is the observed-state marker retained longest on this page. When you see it, first copy the item immediately before it and the item immediately after it, along with its position in the original result. Then stop cleaning up: do not delete the input, change the page to "Handled", or attach a later green result at the original location as a replacement. If someone later identifies a different first divergence, a correction may be added, but retain the old observation as what was seen at the time.

Someone previously attributed `UnprocessedItems` directly to a credentials issue. That claim lacks sufficient supporting material and remains in the old handoff records; it should no longer be used as a decision criterion. It now means only this: preserve the observed state here, and start the next investigation from an earlier or adjacent difference. If it is the earliest difference, write "Stopped at UnprocessedItems" in the handoff entry; if a difference already exists before it, name the earlier object in the entry without repeating this marker.

If the page shows only this marker, with no preceding or following items, preserve it as is and stop. Do not infer queues, requests, or retry counts from the label name, and do not fill in output from elsewhere. The current page does not contain enough records to establish a fixed relationship between this marker and any particular recovery action.

## The Old Stopping Point for `TransferConfig`

An early version said: stop here if `TransferConfig` does not appear. This remains a conservative stopping point for the old environment, because it prevents the incoming operator from continuing on the basis of assumed defaults for fields that are not present. It no longer means "absence means failure", nor does it mean "presence rules out failure".

If this run already has a divergence in the input, version, or first result before `TransferConfig`, prioritize preserving that divergence. Stop at `TransferConfig` as described in the old record only if there are no earlier differences and the comparison depends on this label. When stopping, clearly distinguish two cases: the label was not seen on the page, or there was no material available this time to compare that label. These two statements are not interchangeable.

Do not manually fill in configuration to complete the old form, and do not assert that it should be present in this run just because it was seen in other runs. The old page retains this stopping point precisely so that missing material remains missing, rather than having the on-call operator fill in a seemingly reasonable value on the spot.

## Change Only One Condition

Change only one condition at a time when making comparisons. First choose a condition you can actually control now, save the raw results before and after the action, and then decide whether to perform the next comparison. If both the input and version differ, this is not a single-condition comparison; return to the original state and record them separately, rather than combining two changes into one conclusion.

Do not write "Session normal" or "Credentials normal" when the observation is "No new differences observed". The latter is only an observation from this comparison; the former claims require additional evidence that this page does not contain. Similarly, if the page recovers, write only "Page recovered"; do not infer from this that the first failure has been explained.

Whichever section `Credentials` appears in, first record its position relative to the first divergence. If there is no original snippet, write "Only the label was seen; order unconfirmed". Someone previously treated it as a direct switching condition based on its name; that claim has not been established by the single-run record on this page. Keep it alongside the old paragraph, but do not use it for decisions during the current shift.

Handle `contextParams` the same way: it is a label visible on the page, not a reason to expand the investigation scope automatically. If it appears after the first divergence, do not pursue it yet; if it appears before the divergence, still record only its position, unless a single-condition comparison explicitly uses it as the condition being changed.

## Other Labels in the Records

`BatchWriter`, `RequestItems`, `ServiceDocumenter`, `copy_dynamodb_params`, `ResourceModel`, `PathLike`, and `Waiter` have all appeared in different versions of the on-call text. On this page, they serve as observed-state labels: record whether they were seen, where they were seen, and what was immediately before and after them. Do not infer call relationships from their names, and do not require a label to appear in the current run just because it belongs to an old sample.

One old habit in this section needs to remain documented. Old handoffs often put `BatchWriter` and `RequestItems` on the same line, as though they necessarily belonged to the same step. Handoffs should now record them separately: seeing only the former, seeing only the latter, and seeing both with their order unconfirmed are all valid raw records. Do not merge them to make the record easier to read.

For `ServiceDocumenter`, `ResourceModel`, and `Waiter`, first confirm whether they actually appear on the page or in the snippets saved for this run. If they do not appear, do not write "No impact"; if they appear but are not near the first divergence, do not automatically dig deeper. They may remain in the handoff notes so the incoming operator knows which names appeared on the old page, but they do not form a causal chain for this run.

The old notes on `copy_dynamodb_params` and `PathLike` are especially fragmented. They show only that someone left these words at the edge of the page at the time; there is not enough context to establish whether they relate to this failure. If they are seen again in the current state, preserve the original wording and adjacent content; do not perform migrations, replacements, or rollbacks based on the old notes.

## Logs and Delayed Output

When you see `deferred logging`, preserve the first snippet in which it is visible and the adjacent results. Text that appears later must not be mixed with earlier input and recorded as observations from the same moment. If the page fills in new content after a wait, record it as "Later-added content" and save it separately from the first result; do not overwrite the first result or backfill the later-added content into earlier steps.

If a trace snippet disagrees with the page text, first preserve both pieces of material as is and mark where they disagree. This page does not specify that either one is necessarily correct. The on-call operator's task is to let the next shift know where the first inconsistency is, not to choose between the two pieces of material without evidence.

Some old records treated delayed output as a sign of recovery. That judgment no longer applies: late output shows only that it arrived late, not that the failure has disappeared. The old judgment may remain in the handoff history to help explain why further inspection stopped at the time, but do not use it to end the handling of this run.

## Situations That Require a Pause

Pause further operations in any of the following situations: the original input cannot be preserved; the first result has already been overwritten by a refresh; two conditions were changed at the same time; the first divergence cannot be found; the page contains only a cleaned-up green result; or the recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment. Pausing does not mean closing the issue. At handoff, leave the known locations, missing content, and actions not performed.

Recovery actions for the shared environment have never been developed into reusable steps on this page. If someone requests a rollback, first record the state before rollback, the reason for the request, and whether it was actually performed. If there is no execution record, write "Not executed"; if it was executed without the same comparison conditions as the original run, write "The execution result cannot be compared directly with the original failure". Do not record the request itself as completed recovery.

The old page once put "Restore service" and "Confirm the cause" in the same handoff entry. They should now be written separately. If the page recovers, update only the page recovery status; if the first divergence remains unexplained, leave it unexplained. This prevents the incoming operator from mistaking a temporarily normal state for a confirmed cause.

## Minimum Content to Leave at Handoff

The handoff does not need to retell the entire run. Leave the page entry point, whether the original input was preserved, the current version, whether the first result is still available, the first difference, whether `UnprocessedItems` was seen, whether work stopped because of `TransferConfig`, the single condition already changed, and the actions not performed. "Unconfirmed" is acceptable for any item.

Rejected guesses should also remain, but keep them separate from observations. For example, "Credentials was previously suspected" may be retained; "Credentials caused the failure" must not be written without new material. The value of old guesses is to prevent the next shift from repeating the same unsupported leap, not to turn a guess into a conclusion through repetition.

The incoming operator still opens this page from `docs/adj-session-auth/runbooks/sessions-and-credentials-quality-signal-board-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. If the page entry point works but the attachments are incomplete, first record the stopping point based on the available page; do not borrow run material from other projects to fill the gaps. This on-call page preserves the handling history of a single failed run, and divergences not covered remain unconfirmed.

# Sessions and Credentials Window Checklist

Before the window ends, handle only borrowing at the current entry point, the final output, the timing of the return, and the existing rollback entry point for adj-session-auth. Records of the live state must preserve what was there before the action and the output afterward; add screenshots after handling is complete, and do not let screenshots replace the original text. This checklist does not cover decisions about the release as a whole, nor does it mix in changes outside the window.

## Before Borrowing

1. Open `docs/adj-session-auth/release/sessions-and-credentials-quality-signal-board-pre-window-close-checklist.md` and first find the `RequestItems` that was in use at the time. Copy the original text there, retaining enough surrounding text to identify its context. If you can find only the name but not the full content, record "Original text incomplete"; do not fill in command arguments from memory.
2. Export the current state before borrowing. Save the export separately from the final output collected later: the former shows what was visible when borrowing began, while the latter shows what this operation left behind. Similar filenames, cropped screenshots, or a record reduced to a summary do not count as having both complete outputs.
3. When `PathLike` appears on the borrowed object, do not clean up the directory first. It only indicates that the working state is still there, not that the object has been returned. Keep the location where it appears, the current directory state, and the borrowing action together in the same record, so that it is clear at the end which directory belongs to this window.

Once borrowing has started, do not reorder the original excerpt, change old values into a new format for readability, or overwrite the previous export. The current entry point defines the boundary of this checklist; do not casually include nearby objects that look related in the record unless they actually appear in this operation's output.

## Final Output

4. Immediately after completing the last operation within the window, save the final output, then return the borrowed object. When saving, confirm that the file can be opened, that its content is not blank, and that it is not the pre-borrowing state mistaken for a new result. If only partial logs are available, retain the visible portion and note where the missing content begins; do not fill missing lines with text written up later.
5. Compare the two outputs and check whether `HAS_CRT` actually appears. This item must come from this operation's final output; path names, parameter names, old screenshots, or logs from elsewhere cannot substitute for it. If `HAS_CRT` does not appear, the output cannot be read, or the relationship between the output and the current entry point cannot be confirmed, stop here.
6. When stopping, retain the pre-borrowing state, the last readable output, the trigger location, and the still-identifiable `PathLike` working state. Do not proceed with the return, and do not first perform a rollback to "try it out". A window whose final output was not successfully saved must not be recorded as completed.

If `copy_dynamodb_params` or `deferred logging` appears in the original environment, simply copy the output excerpts containing them verbatim. These two terms are not success markers, and neither can establish the transfer or session status on its own. If only screenshots of the logs remain, clearly note beside each screenshot whether it shows the state before borrowing, the final output, or the state after a failure; if this is unclear, treat it as unconfirmed.

## Return

7. Return the borrowed current entry point only after the final output has been saved and is readable. Before returning it, check again that subsequent actions have not overwritten the output file; after returning it, keep a separate result record and note the time of return. The state before borrowing, the final output, and the state after return must be distinguishable from one another, and must not be combined into a single statement of "handled".
8. If the return fails, the state cannot be determined, or output is missing, stop before the failing action. Preserve the original output and directory state from before and after the failure, and do not repeatedly overwrite the borrowed object. A partial return must not be marked as complete, and do not assume on your own that the action can be retried just because the directory still exists.

Returning is not synonymous with cleaning up the environment. Whether the directory still exists, whether the files are visible, and whether the current entry point has been returned according to the window actions must be recorded separately. If the state after return was not exported, leave that gap; do not fill in the result using the state from before borrowing.

## Rollback stop points

9. When a rollback is needed, execute it only from the rollback entry point already specified in adj-session-auth. If the entry point has not been located, its contents are incomplete, or you cannot confirm that it applies to the current entry point, stop and retain `TODO: The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment.` Do not add fabricated commands to the checklist or record successful results that have not been observed.
10. If the rollback action has been executed, save its output separately, then check that the borrowed object has not been accidentally deleted. If the rollback output is missing, the rollback remains unconfirmed; do not infer that the rollback succeeded from a successful return. If different states appear before and after the rollback, preserve them as they are, and do not rewrite the differences into a single conclusion before the window ends.

Before wrapping up, ask only three things: whether the final output has been saved and is readable; whether the borrowed object has been returned; whether execution really stopped before the rollback entry point in the event of a failure. If any of these cannot be answered, leave the current state as it is and do not mark it as complete. If you need to review the Sessions and Credentials observations from before and after the window, refer back to `DOC-41`; continue to include only window actions, actual output, and stop points here.

# Dependency Freeze Window Decision Record

Leave the dependency freeze window unchanged this round and keep the existing docs-renderer entry point. This is not because the entry point itself is problem-free, but because the available material only supports checking document artifact anomalies against the frozen repository and reproducible inputs. Changing the window would mix existing outputs with new inputs, making it impossible to tell where the link breakage begins.

The decision is to continue collecting anomalies through the existing entry point. For each generation failure, retain at least the generation command, model version, and first page with a broken link. Record success or failure separately for runtime, generated documentation, and the credential boundary; do not treat the result from one as a conclusion about the other two.

"Adjusting the window" has not been rejected; it just won't be done this round. It can reduce waiting during the freeze, but we don't yet have enough samples to show that compatibility in adjacent cases would still be preserved after the adjustment. Keep this proposal on record and revisit it once there are enough documentation reproduction records.

The working assumption is that document artifacts can be handled independently first, and that the credential boundary will not change this judgment. This assumption has not yet been tested with side-by-side records using the same input.
